beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Salary day was three weeks ago. Rohan has already spent ₹40,000, and his account is almost empty. At 6% inflation, in ten years the same month could cost ₹71,634.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Where does it all go? Every single month!

lines.text: Most start on the first two

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Here is the thing. There are six levels of money, and almost everyone starts on the first two.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: By the end, you will know which level you are on, the trap waiting on every floor, and the one move that takes you up.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: And the last level? It is not about earning more. You will see.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Think of it as a road with six signposts. Rohan is standing at the very first one.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: On level one, ₹40,000 comes in, and ₹40,000 goes out. Every single month, back to zero.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rent on the first. Food delivery all week. A friend's wedding on the twentieth. And by the twenty fifth, he is counting coins.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Even Sikka has nothing left to cheer about.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Rohan, what happens if your job stops next month?

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Next month? I would be broke in a week.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And that is normal. Most first jobs start right here, so level one is not a failure. Staying here is the problem.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And a raise alone does not fix it. When the salary goes up, the spending quietly follows. A bigger flat, a nicer phone, more dinners out.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Because here is the trap of level one. Prices never stand still. At 6% inflation a year, the life that costs ₹40,000 a month today will cost ₹71,634.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Watch the cost of the same life climb, year after year. Nothing new in his cart. Just the same rent, the same food, the same bills.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That is ₹31,634 more every month. And over ten years, ₹19.1 L extra, just to live exactly the same life.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: So your salary has to rise every year, just to stand still.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The move off level one is boring, and it works. Spend a little less than you earn, and keep the gap somewhere you will not touch.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Do that for long enough, and he reaches level two. The floor where most people think they are finally safe.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: On level two, six months of spending, ₹2,40,000, sitting safely in a fixed deposit.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: How big should a cushion be? The usual rule is three to six months of spending. Rohan goes for six, because his job is new.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Six months covered! I am basically rich now!

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Not rich, Rohan. Safe. That is a different thing.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And safe matters. If the job stops, the cushion pays the rent while he finds the next one. No loan, no panic, no card.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So level two is a must. But it hides a quiet trap, and it is the reason so many people never climb past it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The fixed deposit pays 7% a year. But prices are rising at 6%. So most of the interest just keeps up with prices.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Ten years go by. He never touches it. The FD keeps renewing, quietly.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: On paper, it has grown to ₹4.7 L. Almost double. It looks wonderful.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: But in today's money, after ten years of rising prices, it buys what ₹2.6 L buys now. The green line is the paper. The red line is what it can actually buy.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: His real growth? About 0.9% a year. Ten years of saving, and his cushion barely grew at all.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And if he had kept it as cash at home? In today's money it would be worth just ₹1.3 L. Rising prices quietly take ₹1.1 L.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: A cushion is for falling on. It was never meant for growing.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So the move on level two: keep the cushion, and stop adding to it once it is full. Every rupee after that needs a different job.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: But first, there is one trap that knocks people from level two straight back down to level one. And it fits in your wallet.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Level three is simple. You owe nobody. Then a festive sale arrives, and Rohan puts ₹50,000 on his credit card.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The bill arrives. Total due, ₹50,000. Minimum due, just ₹2,500.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So he does what millions of people do. He pays the minimum.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Only ₹2,500? Easy. Bill paid!

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: But the card charges 3.5% a month on everything still owed.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That sounds small. Over a year, it is 42%. And because interest lands on interest, it really works out to about 51%.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Twelve months go by. Rohan pays every minimum, on time, not once late.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: By now he has paid ₹27,385. And he still owes ₹40,826.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: What? I paid more than half of it already!

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Because ₹18,211 of what he paid went straight to interest. Only the rest touched the actual debt.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And the minimum shrinks as the balance shrinks, so the road goes on and on. Year after year, the debt walks beside him.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: It takes 183 monthly payments. That is about 15 years.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: All in, he pays ₹1.4 L to clear ₹50,000. That is about 2.9× what he spent.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: In my bank days, we had a name for people who pay only the minimum. Our best customers.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And that is how one sale pushes a person back down. Every month, part of his salary belongs to the card, and he is back on level one.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Even converting the bill into a one year EMI at 16% would cost about ₹4,439 in interest. The minimum road costs ₹93,871.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: The move on level three. Pay the total due every month, with autopay. Never take cash from a card.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: If you truly cannot, a short EMI beats the minimum. And spend on the card only what is already in your account.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So that is three floors. Spend less than you earn. Build the cushion. Owe nobody.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: And on the next floor, something changes. For the first time, your money starts climbing on its own.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: On level four, Rohan invests ₹10,000 a month, every month, for 5 years. Not into the cushion this time, into investments.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The usual way in India is a SIP. A fixed amount goes into a mutual fund on the same date, every month, on autopilot.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: But ₹10,000 every month? That is a lot.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Then start with less. The habit matters more than the amount. Raise it with every raise.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: We will assume 12% a year. That is an assumption, not a promise. Markets swing.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Five years of the same date, the same amount. Good months, bad months, he keeps paying in.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: He put in ₹6.0 L. It is now worth about ₹8.2 L.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That difference, ₹2.2 L, is money he never worked a single shift for.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: It made ₹2.2 L without me doing anything?

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Not without you. You kept paying in, even in the months it went down.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Here is the honest catch. Some years the value will fall, sometimes a lot. The people who climb further are the ones who do not stop.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Why does it grow? Returns earn returns. This year's growth joins the pile, and next year the pile grows on that too.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Like a pile of cash that keeps adding to itself. Small at first. And the longer you leave it, the bigger it gets.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So the move on level four: automate it. The SIP leaves on salary day, before you can spend it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Now watch what happens when you give the very same habit a lot more time.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: On level five, it is ₹15,000 a month, for 20 years. Same idea, just a longer hill.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Twenty years. Four phones, two jobs, one wedding. And the SIP never stops.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: At year ten, the pot has reached ₹34.9 L. Nice, but not life changing. Then the second ten years begin.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: At year twenty, it is ₹1.50 Cr. A crore and a half, from ₹15,000 a month.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: A crorepati? Me?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Now the painful part. Start the same SIP ten years late, and you reach only ₹34.9 L. The same monthly amount.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Same Rohan. Same salary. Same SIP. The only difference is the year he started.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Most of that crore arrives in the last ten years. Waiting does not cost you the first ten years. It costs you the last ten.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Time does the heavy lifting. Not the amount.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And the honest catch. Remember the cushion? Prices keep rising, so a crore in twenty years buys a lot less than a crore today.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So the move on level five is the cheapest one in this whole video. Start now, even small, and do not stop.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And every year you wait, the finish line moves further away. To catch up later, the monthly amount has to be much bigger, right when life gets more expensive.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Five floors now. And the last one is not about having more money. It is about what your money does while you sleep.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Level six. Of that ₹1.50 Cr, only ₹36.0 L ever came from his salary. The other ₹1.14 Cr was the money working.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: This is my floor. My money goes to work before I wake up.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Level six needs a much bigger pot than that. Say ₹8,00,00,000. At an assumed 8% a year, it grows by about ₹64.0 L in a single year.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Twenty years from now, at 6% inflation, Rohan's life costs about ₹15,39,425 a year. The growth is bigger than the bill.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So the money pays the bills, and the job becomes optional?

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: That is the idea. But nobody jumps here. Every floor below has to hold.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And one last honest catch. Returns are never guaranteed, and a bad year can wipe the growth out. So people here spend less than the full growth, and let the rest keep up with prices.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Which is exactly why people on level six still keep the cushion, and still owe nobody. The lower floors never go away.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And Sharma Uncle did not get here in one jump. He climbed every floor, one boring month at a time, for decades.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So level six is three things at once. A cushion. No debt. And a pot so big that its growth covers the bills, with room to spare.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So, which floor are you on? And one move on that floor matters more than all the others.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Now be honest with yourself. Not the level you wish you were on. The one your bank account says you are on today.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Walk the road with Rohan. Each signpost is a floor. Stop at the one that sounds like your life today.

items.text: One: spend less than you earn

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Level one, the month ends before the money. Your move: spend less than you earn.

items.text: One: spend less than you earn

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Level two, you have a cushion. Your move: keep it, and stop there.

items.text: One: spend less than you earn

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Level three, nobody owns your salary. Your move: pay the total due, every single month.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Level four, you invest. Your move: automate it.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Level five, time is on your side. Your move: do not stop.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: And level six, keep every floor below you standing.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And the move that matters most is the cheapest one: start early. Same ₹15,000 a month. Start now, ₹1.50 Cr. Start ten years late, ₹34.9 L.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: I am on level two. Next stop, a card I pay in full, and a SIP on salary day.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: And wherever you are, the next floor is one move away. Not six. Just one.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Just one? Fine. Starting this month.

params.cta: Which level are you on? Comment your number
params.assumption: Assumes 6% inflation, FD 7%, card 3.5% a month, returns 12% (8% at level six), before tax and fees.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Our maths is simplified, before tax and fees, so real life will be messier. So, which level are you on? Comment your number. And follow the panchayat for one money question, settled with real maths.
